awd_titl_txt: Conference: The Quantum System Stability and Reproducibility Workshop (StableQ)
awd_abstract_narration:
Along with the emergence of actual quantum computers, quantum computing is expected to transform science, technology, and society by solving problems intractable for classical computers, including those in chemistry, materials, and finance. However, existing quantum computers face a major obstacle: their results are often unstable over time and difficult to reproduce; this is primarily because of the fluctuating noise in the environment. The stability challenge exists across different qubit technologies, including superconducting qubits, trapped-ion qubits, and neutral atom qubits. To address this pressing challenge, the Quantum System Stability and Reproducibility Workshop (StableQ) was established at the Quantum Week 2023, a conference sponsored by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), followed by its second edition at the IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO) in 2024. The third edition, StableQ 2025, is scheduled to be held in September 2025 at IEEE Quantum Week at the Albuquerque Convention Center in New Mexico. 

This award will support students and researchers to participate in StableQ 2025. The project will bring together experts from academia, industry, and national laboratories to report state-of-the-art developments, exchange ideas and practices, and foster cross-disciplinary research aimed at addressing unstable noise and enabling reproducible quantum computing. The workshop is uniquely positioned to foster collaborative efforts by bringing together experts from hardware, software, and algorithms to tackle key stability issues. Through interactive sessions, participants will identify challenges, prioritize research directions, and address gaps between academia, industry, and national laboratories. Ultimately, this project aims to develop novel techniques, strengthen collaborations in the research community, and deliver scalable, stable, and reproducible quantum computing platforms.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Quantum computers are beginning to move out of research laboratories and into the supercomputing centers where scientists will use them to solve real problems. For this transition to succeed, quantum machines must work reliably alongside today's conventional computers, and the results they produce must be reproducible by other researchers. This award supported a workshop that brought researchers together to tackle these challenges, with a special emphasis on helping students enter this fast-growing field.

The workshop was held on September 3, 2025, in Albuquerque, New Mexico, as part of IEEE Quantum Week 2025, one of the largest international conferences on quantum computing. It was organized jointly with the Quantum-Classical Orchestration for Resilient Engineering (Q-CORE) workshop and continues the StableQ workshop series, which was previously held at IEEE Quantum Week 2023 and at the IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture in 2024. The organizers came from George Mason University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, and Northwestern University. A program committee of 13 experts from universities and national laboratories in the United States and Europe reviewed the submitted research papers.

Intellectual Merit:

The workshop featured two keynote talks and eleven peer-reviewed research papers, which are published in the IEEE Quantum Week 2025 proceedings. The keynote speakers, from Argonne National Laboratory and North Carolina State University, discussed how quantum computers can be connected to supercomputers and how to educate the workforce needed to build dependable quantum systems. The research papers were presented in three sessions. The first session covered how to design and connect combined quantum-classical computing systems, including software platforms that make scientific experiments easier to repeat. The second session covered errors and noise, which are the main obstacles to reliable quantum computing, and methods for measuring and correcting them. The third session covered how to tune and fairly compare quantum algorithms on real hardware. Together, this work helps the research community develop the measurements, tools, and design practices needed to make quantum computers dependable and their results trustworthy.

Broader Impacts:

A central goal of this award was to help students and early-career researchers join the quantum computing research community. Through an open call, the workshop received 22 travel award applications from students ranging from undergraduates to doctoral candidates, studying at universities in the United States and abroad, including institutions with limited access to quantum computing resources, and representing more than ten countries of citizenship. Twelve students were selected, and nine received NSF-funded travel support to attend. The supported students came from nine U.S. universities, both public and private, and included an undergraduate researcher and student authors who presented their own work. At the workshop, they shared their research, received feedback from senior researchers, and connected with experts from universities, national laboratories, and industry, connections that can shape their future careers. By preparing these students to work on making quantum computers reliable, the project contributes to training the skilled workforce that the nation's quantum technology efforts will need.

The workshop also served the broader research community by bringing together people who rarely meet in one place: hardware engineers, software and compiler developers, supercomputing experts, and algorithm designers. This kind of exchange matters because making quantum computers reliable cannot be solved at any single layer of the system. The NSF Program Director attended the workshop and met with the students and organizers, giving the research community a direct channel to share its needs and priorities with a funding agency. In the long run, reliable quantum computers are expected to benefit society in areas such as drug discovery, materials design, and optimization. The workshop papers are available through IEEE Xplore, and the program and list of organizers are publicly available on the Q-CORE website, which acknowledges NSF support.
